You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Life (the life)

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'life' (especially 'the life,' Greek zōē) symbolizes eternal, divine life given by God through Jesus Christ — a qualitatively different existence from mere biological life, consisting in saving relationship and union with God, beginning now and consummated in resurrection. In Johannine usage 'the Life' is also a christological title: Christ himself is the embodiment and source of this life.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 14:6 ('I am the way, and the truth, and the life')",
    "John 11:25 ('I am the resurrection and the life')",
    "John 1:4 ('In him was life, and the life was the light of men')",
    "John 10:10 ('I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly')",
    "John 3:16 ('whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life')",
    "John 17:3 ('this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God')",
    "1 John 5:11-12 ('God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son; whoever has the Son has life')",
    "Colossians 3:4 ('Christ who is your life')",
    "John 5:24-26; 6:35, 48 (bread of life)",
    "Romans 6:4, 23 ('newness of life'; 'the gift of God is eternal life')"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Christological title: 'the Life' refers to the person of Christ himself as the source and embodiment of divine life, not merely a gift he confers.",
      "basis": [
        "John 14:6",
        "John 11:25",
        "John 1:4",
        "1 John 1:1-2 ('the word of life... the life was made manifest')",
        "Colossians 3:4"
      ],
      "prominence": "dominant"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Futurist eschatological reading: 'life' primarily denotes resurrection existence in the age to come (immortality, life after death), with less emphasis on present possession.",
      "basis": [
        "Daniel 12:2",
        "Matthew 25:46",
        "Mark 10:30 ('in the age to come eternal life')",
        "1 Corinthians 15:22, 42-54",
        "Revelation 21:4; 22:1-2"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Realized-eschatology reading: eternal life is a present spiritual quality — knowing God now, new birth, abundant living — emphasized in Johannine scholarship and in pietist/evangelical devotional teaching.",
      "basis": [
        "John 17:3",
        "John 5:24 ('has passed from death to life')",
        "John 10:10",
        "John 3:3-6 (new birth)",
        "Galatians 2:20"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Tree of Life / Edenic symbolism: 'life' as access to immortality and communion with God lost in Eden and restored in Christ and the New Jerusalem; wisdom traditions also call Torah/wisdom a 'tree of life.'",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 2:9; 3:22-24",
        "Proverbs 3:18; 11:30",
        "Revelation 2:7; 22:2, 14, 19"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Covenantal choice reading: 'life' as covenant blessing and obedience set against death/curse — choosing God's way (Deuteronomic and wisdom framing).",
      "basis": [
        "Deuteronomy 30:15-20 ('choose life')",
        "Proverbs 4:4, 22-23",
        "Leviticus 18:5",
        "Psalm 16:11"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Participation/theosis reading (Eastern Orthodox and some Catholic theology): 'life' as sharing in the divine nature and energies of God, mediated sacramentally (especially the Eucharist).",
      "basis": [
        "2 Peter 1:4",
        "John 6:53-57 ('unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man... you have no life in you')",
        "John 1:4",
        "Genesis 2:7"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Anthropological/physical reading: 'life' as breath, soul, or blood — the animating principle of creatures (nephesh, ruach), sometimes treated symbolically in atonement contexts ('the life is in the blood').",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 2:7",
        "Leviticus 17:11, 14",
        "Job 33:4",
        "Ecclesiastes 12:7"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions that 'life'/'the life' in its symbolic-theological sense means eternal divine life (zōē) received through Christ, with the definite-article form ('the Life') widely read as a title of Christ himself, chiefly from John 14:6 and 11:25. The main interpretive variation concerns emphasis rather than substance: present possession vs. future resurrection, personal relationship vs. sacramental participation, and gift vs. person. Scholarly discussion also distinguishes Greek zōē (divine/eternal life), bios (earthly livelihood), and psychē (soul-life), a distinction popularized in commentaries though sometimes overstated in devotional literature. None of these alternatives displaces the core consensus."
}

RESPONSE B
{
  "primary_meaning": "Eternal life, spiritual vitality, and the person of Jesus Christ Himself as the source of divine life and salvation (often distinguishing the Greek 'zoe' from mere physical 'bios').",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 14:6",
    "John 1:4",
    "John 11:25",
    "1 John 5:11-12",
    "John 10:10"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Physical existence, breath, or earthly duration.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 2:7",
        "James 4:14"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The Holy Spirit's animating and regenerating power.",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 8:2",
        "John 6:63"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The soul or vital animating force residing in the blood, tied to atonement.",
      "basis": [
        "Leviticus 17:11",
        "Deuteronomy 12:23"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "In biblical theology, particularly in the New Testament and overwhelmingly in Johannine literature, 'the life' symbolizes eternal, divine existence and fellowship with God. Christ is frequently identified not just as the giver of life, but as the personification of 'the life' itself."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "Divine or eternal life given by God in and through Jesus Christ—salvation understood as restored communion with God, spiritually present now and fulfilled in resurrection.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 1:4 — “In him was life,” associating life with the incarnate Word.",
    "John 5:21, 24-26 — the Son gives life and possesses life in himself; believers pass from death to life.",
    "John 10:10, 28 — Jesus gives abundant and eternal life.",
    "John 11:25-26 — Jesus declares, “I am the resurrection and the life.”",
    "John 14:6 — Jesus declares, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”",
    "John 17:3 — eternal life is defined relationally as knowing the Father and Jesus Christ.",
    "Romans 6:4, 23 — believers walk in newness of life, and God’s gift is eternal life in Christ.",
    "Colossians 3:3-4 — Christ is identified as the believer’s life.",
    "1 John 1:1-2; 5:11-12, 20 — eternal life is manifested in Christ and possessed through the Son."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Christ himself as “the Life,” emphasizing his identity as the source, embodiment, and mediator of divine life rather than merely a gift he bestows.",
      "basis": [
        "John 11:25",
        "John 14:6",
        "Colossians 3:4",
        "1 John 1:1-2"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Ordinary created or biological life—the animating breath and earthly existence bestowed and sustained by God. In many passages “life” is literal rather than symbolic.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 2:7",
        "Job 33:4",
        "Psalm 104:29-30",
        "Acts 17:25, 28"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Resurrection life: bodily life restored after death, especially through participation in Christ’s resurrection.",
      "basis": [
        "John 5:28-29",
        "John 11:25-26",
        "Romans 6:4-9",
        "1 Corinthians 15:20-23, 42-49"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Present spiritual renewal or sanctified conduct—“newness of life,” often contrasted with sin, alienation, or spiritual death.",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 6:4, 11-13",
        "Romans 8:6, 10-11",
        "Ephesians 2:1-5",
        "Galatians 2:20"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Covenant flourishing, wisdom, and righteousness: life as well-being, blessing, and the fruitful path produced by fidelity to God.",
      "basis": [
        "Deuteronomy 30:15-20",
        "Proverbs 3:16-18",
        "Proverbs 8:35",
        "Proverbs 12:28",
        "Psalm 16:11"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The Holy Spirit’s life-giving presence or power, particularly as the principle of spiritual and resurrection life.",
      "basis": [
        "John 6:63",
        "Romans 8:2, 6, 10-11",
        "2 Corinthians 3:6"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Immortality or unending conscious existence considered chiefly as duration rather than communion with God or participation in Christ.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:46",
        "John 3:16",
        "Revelation 21:4"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a strong central Christian association between “life,” especially “the life” in Johannine or Christological language, and eternal/divine life in Christ. Nevertheless, the term is highly context-dependent and often denotes ordinary existence, present spiritual renewal, righteous flourishing, or bodily resurrection. Thus there is no single settled symbolic interpretation applicable to every biblical occurrence."
}

RESPONSE D
{
  "primary_meaning": "Jesus Christ himself as the personal source, embodiment, and giver of spiritual/eternal life (zoe)",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 14:6 ('I am the way, and the truth, and the life')",
    "John 11:25 ('I am the resurrection and the life')",
    "John 1:4 ('In him was life')",

        "Leviticus 17:11",

        "Romans 8:2, 10–11",
        "2 Corinthians 3:6"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The Tree of Life as eschatological symbol of immortality and restored paradise",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 2:9; 3:22–24",
        "Revelation 2:7; 22:2, 14"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "In New Testament usage and historic Christian teaching the definite form 'the life' most consistently functions as a christological title or as the divine/eternal life that is identical with or flows from Christ; physical life and the Tree of Life remain important but secondary symbolic registers. The distinction between zoe (divine life) and bios/psyche (creaturely life) is widely recognized in biblical studies."
}

BOOK ENTRY
Covenant existence — the life lived walking in the Way according to God's law.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and the eternal life imparted to believers.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Deut 30:19-20; Lev 18:5; John 14:6; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Deuteronomy 30:19 — I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live:
Deuteronomy 30:20 — That thou mayest love the LORD thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life, and the length of thy days: that thou mayest dwell in the land which the LORD sware unto thy fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
